screens.title: Unit Testing with pytest
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn why many Python projects prefer pytest and how to use its most productive features. We'll start by contrasting pytest with the built-in unittest framework so you see the trade-offs. Then you'll write tests that use plain assert statements, learn how fixtures provide reusable setup and teardown, and discover how @pytest. mark. parametrize reduces duplication. We'll also practice asserting exceptions, controlling fixture scope, and using markers to run only the tests you want. Along the way you'll see a familiar BankAccount example refactored to pytest, and a hands-on activity that uses parameterized tests for a string reverser. This matters because test clarity speeds debugging, fixtures make tests easier to maintain, and parameterization keeps your test suite compact while improving coverage. By the end you'll be able to run pytest, interpret its assertion introspection, and start migrating small test modules from unittest to pytest idioms. As you work, watch for common pitfalls like using the wrong fixture scope or mixing unittest-style assertions with pytest's plain assert mindset. Ready to explore pytest and make your tests simpler and more powerful?

screens.title: pytest vs unittest
screens.narratorSegment: pytest and unittest both let you test Python code, but they differ in style and ergonomics. unittest is built in and uses TestCase classes and assertion methods such as assertEqual. That structure works, but it can add boilerplate for simple tests. pytest encourages plain functions and uses Python's assert keyword. pytest rewrites asserts to produce rich failure messages, so you see both sides of a failing expression without extra method calls. Practically, this means fewer lines of test code and easier reading. Another difference is fixtures: unittest uses setUp and tearDown methods tied to classes; pytest provides fixtures that are regular functions and are injected into tests by name. Fixtures support scopes and composition, which helps manage shared resources. Discovery is different too: pytest finds test files and functions by naming patterns, while unittest discovery can be more manual when you use test loaders. A common misconception is that pytest is less powerful; in reality it is more extensible through plugins and markers. As an example, converting a simple TestCase with setUp to a pytest fixture reduces boilerplate and leads to more focused tests. Consider this comparison a practice in choosing clarity and speed of test authoring.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › pytest vs unittest
unittest
Class-based, explicit setup
Uses TestCase, setUp/tearDown methods, and assertion methods like assertEqual. Good for some structured cases, but adds ceremony for small tests.
Example pattern
import unittest

class TestAccount(unittest.TestCase):
  def setUp(self):
    self.account = BankAccount(100)

  def test_deposit(self):
    self.account.deposit(50)
    self.assertEqual(self.account.balance, 150)
pytest
Function-based, lightweight asserts
Write tests as simple functions, use plain assert, and define fixtures as reusable setup. Less boilerplate and clearer failures.
Equivalent example
def test_deposit():
  account = BankAccount(100)
  account.deposit(50)
  assert account.balance == 150
Less boilerplate
Flexible fixtures
Powerful plugins

screens.title: Plain assert and assertion rewriting
screens.narratorSegment: A defining feature of pytest is its support for plain Python assert statements. When an assert fails, pytest rewrites the expression to show the left and right values, making it much easier to diagnose errors than manually calling assertion methods. Practically, that means you write fewer framework-specific lines and more straightforward Python. For example, instead of calling an assertEqual method, you simply assert that account. balance equals an expected number. pytest will display the evaluated expression and intermediate values on failure. A useful concrete example is our BankAccount deposit test: write assert account. balance == 150 and, if the test fails, pytest prints the actual balance as part of the failure output. Misconceptions to avoid: assert is not weaker than assertion methods — pytest's rewriting preserves detailed diagnostics. Another subtlety is not to shadow built-in assert behavior with custom assertion functions; prefer direct expressions for clarity. Let's look at the test file that uses plain asserts; read it to see how readability improves. After you run pytest, inspect a failing assertion message to learn which part of your expression is incorrect. That feedback loop shortens the time from failure to fix.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Plain assert and assertion rewriting
Test using plain assert
import pytest
from account import BankAccount

def test_deposit():
    account = BankAccount(100)
    account.deposit(50)
    assert account.balance == 150
If this assertion fails, pytest shows the left and right values so you can see the actual balance immediately.
Why this helps
  • Less framework code: write standard Python instead of assertion method calls.
  • Readable failures: pytest expands the expression to show intermediate values.
  • Faster debugging loop: see concrete mismatches immediately and fix the implementation or test.
Common mistake
Using assert with side effects inside complex expressions can make failures harder to interpret. Keep assertions focused and explicit.

test_account_pytest.py
import pytest
from account import BankAccount

def test_initial_balance():
    account = BankAccount(100)
    assert account.balance == 100

def test_deposit():
    account = BankAccount(100)
    account.deposit(50)
    assert account.balance == 150

def test_deposit_zero_or_negative_amount_raises_error():
    account = BankAccount(100)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        account.deposit(0)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        account.deposit(-10)

def test_withdraw_insufficient_funds_raises_error():
    account = BankAccount(50)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        account.withdraw(100)

screens.title: Fixtures: setup and teardown
screens.narratorSegment: Fixtures are reusable functions that provide setup and optional teardown for tests. Instead of using a setUp method on a TestCase, you define a function decorated with @pytest. fixture and return or yield the resource. pytest injects the fixture into tests by matching its name to a test function argument. For example, a default_account fixture can create a BankAccount with an initial balance and yield it. Code after yield runs as teardown, letting you close resources or print messages. Fixtures improve test clarity because each test declares exactly which resources it needs through function arguments, making dependencies explicit and easy to reuse across many tests. A common misconception is that fixtures hide setup logic; in truth they make it visible and sharable. Another pitfall is forgetting to request the fixture in the test signature—without the name in the function arguments, pytest won’t inject it. We’ll also cover fixture scopes in the next screen, because choosing function versus module or session scope affects isolation and performance. Use fixtures for shared construction and controlled teardown, but keep them small and focused so tests remain readable and predictable.

keyIdea.title: Fixture fundamentals
keyIdea.text: Define @pytest.fixture functions and request them by name in test signatures to share setup and teardown cleanly across tests.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Fixtures: setup and teardown
Fixture example
import pytest
from account import BankAccount

@pytest.fixture
def default_account():
    print("Setting up default_account fixture.")
    account = BankAccount(100)
    yield account
    print("Tearing down default_account fixture.")

def test_deposit_with_fixture(default_account):
    default_account.deposit(50)
    assert default_account.balance == 150
Fixture benefits
  • Explicit dependencies: tests declare what they need by name.
  • Reusable setup: one function used by many tests keeps code DRY.
  • Yield-based teardown: cleanup code runs after the test that requested the fixture.
Common mistake
Forgetting to include the fixture name in the test signature prevents injection — pytest will not call the fixture silently.

screens.title: Fixture scopes and isolation
screens.narratorSegment: Fixture scope determines how often pytest sets up and tears down a fixture. The most common scope is function, which runs before and after each test that requests the fixture. Function scope provides maximum isolation. Module scope creates a single fixture instance for all tests in a module, speeding tests when shared state is safe. Class scope ties fixtures to test classes, and session scope creates one instance for the entire test run, useful for expensive, global resources. The practical decision is about isolation versus performance: prefer function scope for mutable state to avoid flakiness, and use module or session scope when resource setup is costly and tests do not mutate the resource. A concrete example: if a fixture opens a database connection and tests reset data between runs, module scope may be acceptable; if tests mutate shared state without resetting, function scope is safer. A common pitfall is accidentally using a broad scope that shares state between tests, causing order-dependent failures. Always consider teardown behavior and explicit resets when choosing scope. When in doubt, pick function scope during development and optimize scope later once tests are stable.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Fixture scopes and isolation
Fixture scope comparison
function
Runs per test. Best isolation.
class
Runs once per test class.
module
Runs once per module. Faster when safe.
session
Runs once per test run. Use for costly global resources.
Practical checklist
  • If tests mutate fixture state, prefer function scope for isolation.
  • For expensive, read-only resources, consider module or session scope.
  • When optimizing, measure test runtime and change scope intentionally with clear teardown.

screens.title: Asserting exceptions with pytest.raises
screens.narratorSegment: When a test must verify that a particular operation raises an exception, pytest provides pytest. raises as a clear, readable context manager. Instead of wrapping code in try-except and asserting failure, write with pytest. raises(ValueError): followed by the call that should raise. This pattern expresses intent directly and yields compact tests. For example, to test that withdrawing more money than the balance raises a ValueError, create a BankAccount with a small balance and inside the with block call withdraw with an excessive amount. If the code does not raise the expected exception, the test fails and pytest prints a helpful message. A common misconception is that pytest. raises hides the exception details; in fact, you can capture the caught exception by assigning the context manager to a variable for additional checks on the exception message. Also, do not put multiple unrelated calls inside the same pytest. raises block; keep each assertion focused. This approach improves readability and makes it obvious which call should raise. Use pytest. raises whenever you need to assert error behavior in your code. Asserting exceptions with pytest.raises means use with pytest.raises(expectedexception) to assert that a specific call raises the expected error, keeping tests concise and intent-revealing.. In practical terms, use a context manager to assert that code raises the expected exception. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › pytest.raises
Example: withdraw error
import pytest
from account import BankAccount

def test_withdraw_insufficient_funds_raises_error():
    account = BankAccount(50)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        account.withdraw(100)
This makes it clear that withdraw is expected to raise a ValueError for insufficient funds.
Advanced: inspect message
def test_error_message():
    account = BankAccount(0)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError) as excinfo:
        account.withdraw(10)
    assert "Insufficient funds" in str(excinfo.value)
Tip: capture the exception to assert on its message or attributes when needed.

screens.title: Parameterize tests with @pytest.mark.parametrize
screens.narratorSegment: Parameterized tests let you run the same logic with multiple inputs and expected outputs without copying code. Use @pytest. mark. parametrize to declare parameter names and a list of value tuples. pytest runs the test once per tuple, reporting each combination as a separate test case. This is ideal for validating functions across many scenarios, such as deposit and withdraw operations or a string reverser with many sample inputs. For example, a deposit test can accept initial balance, deposit amount, and expected balance; parametrize provides three rows and the test executes three times. Parameterization reduces test maintenance and makes it easier to add new cases. A common misuse is putting too many parameters into a single test that becomes hard to read—keep parameter sets focused and name variables clearly. Another tip: when a specific data combination needs special handling, prefer a separate test to keep failures easy to interpret. Parameterize is especially useful for data-driven tests and increases coverage with minimal code. We'll show concrete code using both bank account examples and the string reverser practice so you can copy the pattern directly.

screens.title: Running pytest and interpreting output
screens.narratorSegment: Running pytest is simple: install it with pip, open a terminal in your project directory, and run the pytest command. pytest searches files by the test_* dot P Y file and *_test dot P Y file patterns and collects functions and methods beginning with test_. When tests run, pytest prints a concise summary and, on failure, shows a detailed report with the failing assertion, evaluated values, and stack trace. This output helps you determine whether the failure is in the test or the code under test. A typical developer flow is: run pytest, inspect failures, fix code or adjust tests, and re-run. Use -k to run tests matching an expression, -m to run markers, and -q for quieter output. For debugging, -s shows print output and -vv increases verbosity. A misconception is expecting pytest to run only changed tests automatically; it runs everything unless you scope the run or use tools that select modified tests. Also, markers let you group slow or integration tests so you can run quick unit tests during development and slower tests in CI. Learning to read pytest's assertion output is a key skill — it saves time by showing the evaluated subexpressions and the exact line that failed.

screens.title: Pitfalls and migration tips
screens.narratorSegment: When adopting pytest, several common mistakes show up. First, forgetting to install pytest means tests won't run; install with pip before running tests. Second, carrying over unittest habits like relying on TestCase methods or assert methods leads to unnecessary complexity — prefer function-based tests and plain assert. Third, mishandling fixture scope can create shared-state bugs; avoid session scope for mutable fixtures unless you clean state explicitly. Fourth, placing multiple assertions or unrelated calls in a single pytest. raises block obscures which operation should raise. Fifth, naming files or functions incorrectly prevents discovery — use test_ prefixes or suffixes. As you migrate tests, don't simply wrap TestCase classes; instead refactor into focused functions and small fixtures. Also avoid heavy use of global mutable fixtures; prefer yields with teardown or explicit reset between tests. A good migration strategy is to convert one small module at a time, run tests, and adjust fixture scopes as needed. Keep tests readable and intentional: a clear test failure is the fastest route to a fix. We'll also practice asserting exceptions, controlling fixture scope, and using markers to run only the tests you want. Along the way you'll see a familiar BankAccount example refactored to pytest, and a hands-on activity that uses parameterized tests for a string reverser. This matters because test clarity speeds debugging, fixtures make tests easier to maintain, and parameterization keeps your test suite compact while improving coverage. By the end you'll be able to run pytest, interpret its assertion introspection, and start migrating small test modules from unittest to pytest idioms. As you work, watch for common pitfalls like using the wrong fixture scope or mixing unittest-style assertions with pytest's plain assert mindset. Ready to explore pytest and make your tests simpler and more powerful?

I'll show you a concrete BankAccount example refactored from unittest to pytest so you can see the practical benefits. Second, you'll write tests using plain assert statements and understand how pytest rewrites them to produce helpful failure messages, which makes debugging faster. Third, you'll use fixtures to manage setup and teardown: you'll create a fixture that returns a BankAccount, watch how pytest injects it into tests, and learn common fixture scopes. Finally, you'll implement parameterized tests using @pytest. mark. parametrize to run the same test logic with many input sets, saving duplication and improving coverage. Each objective pairs a small example with an explanation of why it matters in larger codebases. We'll also point out typical mistakes like incorrect fixture scope or trying to keep unittest habits. By meeting these goals you'll have practical skills to write cleaner, more maintainable tests that scale with your project.

These secondary objectives focus on practical execution and avoiding common errors. You'll learn how pytest discovers tests so you can structure file and function names for automatic discovery. We'll practice using pytest. raises as a context manager to assert exceptions, which leads to clearer intent than try-except checks. You'll also learn how to mark tests with custom markers for selective execution, useful when running slow or integration tests separately from fast unit tests. Finally, we'll cover migrating habits from unittest: embrace function-based tests and fixture injection instead of class-based setup, and avoid mixing unittest assertion methods with pytest's plain assert. Each objective includes a small example and a misconception check so you can diagnose errors quickly. For example, using session-scoped fixtures when tests require isolation can cause subtle shared state bugs — we'll show how to pick scope thoughtfully. These skills help you run targeted tests, write clearer failure assertions, and design tests that are easier to maintain in real projects.

pytest and unittest both let you test Python code, but they differ in style and ergonomics. unittest is built in and uses TestCase classes and assertion methods such as assertEqual. That structure works, but it can add boilerplate for simple tests. pytest encourages plain functions and uses Python's assert keyword. pytest rewrites asserts to produce rich failure messages, so you see both sides of a failing expression without extra method calls. Practically, this means fewer lines of test code and easier reading. Another difference is fixtures: unittest uses setUp and tearDown methods tied to classes; pytest provides fixtures that are regular functions and are injected into tests by name. Fixtures support scopes and composition, which helps manage shared resources. Discovery is different too: pytest finds test files and functions by naming patterns, while unittest discovery can be more manual when you use test loaders. A common misconception is that pytest is less powerful; in reality it is more extensible through plugins and markers. As an example, converting a simple TestCase with setUp to a pytest fixture reduces boilerplate and leads to more focused tests. Consider this comparison a practice in choosing clarity and speed of test authoring.

A defining feature of pytest is its support for plain Python assert statements. When an assert fails, pytest rewrites the expression to show the left and right values, making it much easier to diagnose errors than manually calling assertion methods. Practically, that means you write fewer framework-specific lines and more straightforward Python. For example, instead of calling an assertEqual method, you simply assert that account. balance equals an expected number. pytest will display the evaluated expression and intermediate values on failure. Let's look at the test file that uses plain asserts; read it to see how readability improves. After you run pytest, inspect a failing assertion message to learn which part of your expression is incorrect. That feedback loop shortens the time from failure to fix.
